# The Festival and the Collar

The raspberry tart was too sweet.

Throné set it down on the wooden table and watched Agnea devour hers in three bites, crumbs tumbling onto the front of her dress. The girl didn't notice. She was too busy scanning the Festival Grounds, taking in the banners strung between the trees, the lanterns swaying in the evening breeze, the children chasing each other between the food stalls.

"Isn't it wonderful?" Agnea said, brushing ineffectually at the crumbs. "Everyone's smiling. Papa says this is the best turnout we've had in years."

Throné followed her gaze across the clearing. The villagers did look happy—farmers and their families, an old woman selling peach preserves, a cluster of young men arguing cheerfully over who would win the raspberry-eating contest. The kind of people who went to bed when the sun set and rose with the dawn, who had never needed to learn which rooftops in a city could bear your weight when you were running from a mark gone wrong.

"It's loud," Throné said.

Agnea's face fell for half a second before she rallied. "Well, that's what makes it a festival! The noise is part of the fun. You'll see—once the music starts and people get dancing, you'll feel it."

Throné doubted that, but she didn't say so. Agnea had been so eager when she'd invited her, those brown eyes bright with the kind of hope that didn't know how to quit. *You have to come to Cropdale. There's a festival, and I'm performing, and you'll love it, I promise.* Throné had meant to refuse. Cropdale was small, too open, too far from any place she could disappear if she needed to. But Agnea had touched the rose on her headband, the way she did when she was nervous, and Throné had heard herself saying yes.

She was still figuring out what to do with people who wanted her around for reasons that had nothing to do with a contract or a key.

"Your father seems well," Throné said, because Agnea was looking at her expectantly.

"He is! He's been working so hard on the costumes for tonight. Half the village wanted something special made, and he's been sewing till his fingers ache." Agnea leaned forward, lowering her voice. "He's nervous about me performing again. He tries to hide it, but I can tell. He still thinks I'm going to work myself to death like Mama did."

"Will you?"

Agnea blinked. "What? No! I mean—I'm careful now. I know when to rest. And besides, I'm not alone anymore. I have all of you."

*All of you.* The eight travelers. The people who had walked into the dark and fought a god and somehow walked back out. Throné still wasn't used to the idea that she was part of that *you*, that she had a place in it that wasn't provisional or purchased.

Osvald, who had grown up in Flamechurch among the clerics of the Sacred Flame, had once told her that every festival was a ritual with better food.

A small girl darted past their table, nearly colliding with Throné's chair. Agnea caught her by the shoulder.

"Careful, now! You'll trip."

The girl looked up, wide-eyed. "Sorry, Miss Agnea." Then she was gone, weaving back into the crowd.

"That's Melle," Agnea said. "She's Gus's niece. Sweet girl, but she's got two left feet. Reminds me of myself."

Throné had seen Agnea trip over her own heels a dozen times, seen her pick herself back up with that bright, unshakable smile. It should have been irritating. Somehow it wasn't.

"You're staring," Agnea said.

"Hmm." Throné looked away, toward the raised stage at the center of the grounds. "When do you perform?"

"Sundown. That's when the festival really starts." Agnea's voice dropped, turning shy. "I'm a little nervous, actually. I haven't performed here since the night I left home. What if I've gotten worse? What if they're expecting the girl who won the Grand Gala and I just… stumble?"

"You won't."

"You don't know that."

"I do." Throné met her eyes. "You didn't stumble when we fought Vide. You won't stumble here."

Agnea's cheeks colored. She touched her headband again. "That's—that's different. That was life and death. This is just a festival."

"Is it?"

For a moment Agnea was quiet, worrying her lower lip. Then she laughed, a soft sound. "You're right. It's not just a festival. It's home. That makes it scarier, somehow."

Throné understood that. She thought of the backstreets of New Delsta, the weight of the collar around her neck, the way every familiar street corner had felt like a trap. Home could be the most dangerous place of all.

Even now she still answered to the Blacksnakes, slipping away whenever Mother sent word.

"You should go," Throné said. "Find your father. Check your costume."

"What about you?"

"I'll be here."

Agnea hesitated, then reached across the table and squeezed Throné's hand. Her palm was warm, slightly sticky from the raspberry tart. "Thank you for coming. I know this isn't your kind of place."

"It's fine."

"It's not, but you came anyway." Agnea stood, smoothing her skirt. "I'll find you after, all right? We can watch the stars together once the dancing's done."

She hurried off toward the village, her braid bouncing against her back. Throné watched her go, then looked down at her own hand. She could still feel the ghost of Agnea's touch, the easy warmth of it. No one had held her hand like that since—

She stopped the thought. Stood. The festival was growing more crowded as the sun sank lower, families claiming spots near the stage, vendors calling out their wares. Throné moved to the edge of the clearing where the trees started, her back to an old oak, and watched.

She bought a cup of cider from Orrin, the bald bartender who had set up a barrel beside the stage.

An hour passed. The sky bled orange, then purple. Lanterns were lit. A fiddler took the stage, joined by a drummer, and the music started—fast, bright, relentless. Villagers began to dance, clumsy and joyful, stomping in time. Throné's head started to ache.

Then Agnea appeared on stage, and the crowd roared.

She wore her mother's dress, the black bodice and orange skirt catching the lantern light, the cyan sash bright as a river. The rose in her headband seemed to glow. She stood at the center of the stage, head high, and for a moment she was completely still.

Then she moved.

Throné had seen Agnea dance before—in taverns, on city streets, once in the ruins of an old temple while they were fleeing from a pack of shaggy aurochs. But this was different. This was Agnea dancing for people who had known her since she was a child, who remembered her mother, who had watched her trip over her own feet a thousand times and still believed in her. Every step was precise, deliberate. Her arms swept wide, her skirt flared, and she spun, once, twice, three times without faltering.

The crowd clapped in rhythm. Agnea began to sing, her voice clear and high, and Throné recognized the melody—the *Song of Hope*, the one Gil had written for her in New Delsta. The words were about new dawns and second chances, about stumbling and rising and shining anyway.

It should have been saccharine. It should have made Throné want to leave.

Instead, she found herself unable to look away.

Agnea danced like she was calling the sun back from the edge of the world, like every movement mattered, like hope was something you could pour into a person just by showing them you hadn't given up. And the villagers—these simple, tired farmers—watched her with something like reverence.

Throné thought of Claude, of the way he had looked at her like she was a vessel to be filled. She thought of Mother's whip, of Father's dagger, of Pirro's last question. *What do you want?*

She thought of the dawn they had fought for, the one Agnea had helped them win.

Even Hikari had sent a letter from the kingdom of Sai, which he now ruled, wishing Agnea luck tonight.

The song ended. Agnea held the final note, arms stretched toward the darkening sky, and the crowd erupted. People were shouting her name, children were jumping, and an older man—Garud, Throné realized—was wiping his eyes.

Agnea took her bow, stumbled slightly on the way down, and laughed at herself. The crowd laughed with her, not cruel but fond, and she waved before disappearing backstage.

Throné let out a breath she hadn't realized she'd been holding.

"She's something, isn't she?"

Throné turned. A young man had approached—Gus, the tavern owner, the one who had gone into the forest with Agnea to fight the duorduor. He was holding two cups of something that smelled like cider.

"She is," Throné said.

"I've known her since we were kids," Gus said, offering one of the cups. Throné shook her head. "She used to practice her dancing in the tavern after closing, just her and the empty chairs. Tripped over her own feet every other step. But she never stopped trying." He took a sip. "I'm glad she found people who see what I see."

Throné didn't know what to say to that, so she said nothing.

Gus smiled. "She's looking for you, by the way. Said to tell you she'll meet you by the old bridge, north of here. Less crowded."

He wandered off before Throné could answer.

She slipped through the crowd, past the food stalls and the dancing villagers, and followed the path north. The noise of the festival faded behind her. The bridge was small, wooden, spanning a narrow stream. Agnea was already there, sitting on the railing with her legs dangling, her heeled shoes discarded beside her.

Lantern light spilled from the Copper Kettle, a little tavern at the edge of the grounds, as she passed.

"There you are," Agnea said. "I was worried you'd left."

"I said I'd be here."

"I know. But crowds aren't your thing." Agnea patted the railing beside her. "Come sit."

Throné hesitated, then climbed up. The wood was cool beneath her, the night air soft. Below them the stream burbled, dark and quick. Agnea was quiet for a moment, looking up at the stars beginning to prick through the sky.

"Did you like it?" she asked finally.

"You didn't stumble."

Agnea laughed. "I almost did. During the third spin. But I caught myself." She swung her feet, the motion idle, content. "It felt good. Being home. Showing them I did what I said I would."

Throné thought of Lostseed, of the hollow-eyed people and the crying baby, of the place that should have been home but had only ever been a cage.

"You're lucky," Throné said.

"I know." Agnea glanced at her. "But you have a home now too, don't you? With us. The eight of us. We're a strange family, but we're family."

"Hmm."

"I mean it." Agnea's voice turned fierce. "You're not alone anymore. You don't have to be."

Throné looked at her—this girl who tripped over her own feet, who believed in new dawns and second chances, who had invited a killer to a village festival because she wanted her to see people smile. Agnea was still wearing the rose headband, her mother's good-luck charm. The kind of thing Throné would have stolen once, appraised, and sold.

Now it just looked like love.

"Thank you," Throné said quietly.

Agnea blinked. "For what?"

"For inviting me."

"Oh." Agnea's smile softened. "You don't have to thank me for that. I wanted you here."

They sat together in silence, listening to the stream and the distant music. Agnea started humming the *Song of Hope* under her breath, the melody threading through the night. Throné closed her eyes and let herself feel it—the cool air, the sound of water, the presence of someone who wanted nothing from her except her company.

It didn't erase the blood. It didn't undo the years of the collar or the people she'd killed or the way her hands still remembered how to hold a blade.

But it was something.

After a while, Agnea stopped humming. "Néné calls you that sometimes. Néné."

"Ochette calls you Aggie."

"She does." Agnea kicked her feet again. "Do you have a nickname? Something people called you before?"

Throné thought of the Blacksnakes, of Mother's lash and Father's lessons. No one had called her anything but her name. Names were for control, not affection.

"No," she said.

"Well," Agnea said, "maybe that's all right. You get to start fresh. Decide who you want to be."

Throné opened her eyes. Agnea was looking at her with that bright, unshakable hope, the kind that made you think maybe the dawn was worth fighting for after all.

"Maybe," Throné said.

Agnea grinned. "Come on. Let's go back. They're about to start the raspberry-eating contest, and Pala says she's going to beat the record this year. You have to see it."

She hopped down from the railing, wobbled, and caught herself on the bridge post. Throné climbed down after her, steadier, and Agnea threaded her arm through Throné's without asking.

"Let's go," Agnea said, tugging her forward.

And Throné, who had spent twenty-three years learning how to slip free from every hold, let herself be led back toward the lights.
